# **Forensic Computer Vision Architecture for Municipal Work Evidence Verification: An Instance-Level Copy Detection and Provenance Pipeline**

## **Architectural Disambiguation: Instance-Level Copy Detection Versus Semantic Similarity**

Visual evidence verification within municipal audit frameworks serves a fundamentally distinct operational objective from general-purpose computer vision tasks like semantic search, image classification, or zero-shot retrieval1. In municipal contract governance, auditing bodies must verify photographic proof submitted by contractors to substantiate public works billing across infrastructure domains, including asphalt resurfacing, pothole remediation, storm-drain maintenance, and structural repair4. A pervasive vulnerability in these workflows is photographic fraud, wherein contractors submit duplicate images across multiple invoices, re-upload historical evidence from completed work orders, introduce geometric crops or rotations to evade basic deduplication, or digitally splice elements into photographs to simulate work that was never performed3.

Deploying generic semantic foundation models such as Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining (CLIP) or standard Vision Transformers like DINOv2 to address this problem represents an architectural mismatch6. Semantic vision models are explicitly optimized to map images sharing conceptual content into identical representation clusters within the embedding space6. Under CLIP or vanilla DINOv2, two completely independent photographs of asphalt defects located in disparate districts will exhibit near-identical latent representations because their visual embeddings are optimized around high-level semantic abstractions of damaged aggregate and road wear6. Consequently, deploying semantic models in municipal auditing yields unacceptable false-positive rates, erroneously flagging distinct municipal sites as fraudulent copies simply because they share visual textures, municipal equipment, or environmental settings3.

Conversely, Instance-Level Image Copy Detection (ICD) enforces the strict condition that an embedding vector must match only images originating from the identical physical exposure and camera sensor act, irrespective of post-capture digital manipulations1. The latent space must remain strictly invariant to content-preserving transformations, such as aggressive spatial cropping, lossy compression, perspective shifts, photometric jitter, and synthetic overlays, while remaining discriminatively orthogonal across distinct physical scenes that share identical semantic categories1.

Classical perceptual hashing algorithms, including perceptual hash (pHash) and difference hash (dHash), provide high computational throughput and compact representations, but fail under adversarial or real-world image modifications. Perceptual hashing maps low-frequency Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) coefficients or local spatial gradients to 64-bit binary strings. While pHash exhibits resilience against minor photometric alterations and mild compression, it is fragile under spatial transformations: a crop discarding more than 15% of the frame or an unaligned rotation of even a few degrees catastrophically disrupts the global spatial frequency layout, causing Hamming distances to exceed standard match thresholds.

Local feature descriptors such as SIFT, SURF, and ORB paired with geometric verification through Random Sample Consensus (RANSAC) provide spatial invariance against rotations, scale alterations, and partial occlusions12. However, storing and indexing unaggregated local descriptors across hundreds of thousands of municipal work photographs introduces severe storage and latency bottlenecks12. Matching hundreds of local keypoint vectors per image across enterprise archives requires complex inverted multi-index architectures that degrade query latency beyond interactive operational limits13.

Modern self-supervised copy-detection networks, specifically Meta AI's Self-Supervised Descriptor (SSCD), resolve this architectural trade-off1. By utilizing contrastive learning objectives regularized through differential entropy and paired with domain-specific augmentation pipelines, SSCD generates compact, globally aggregated vectors that yield distinct separation between authentic visual copies and deceptive semantic distractors1.

## **Representation Learning and Embedding Architecture**

### **Core Feature Extraction Model**

The optimal model for MuniAudit-AI's visual copy-detection core is Meta AI's Self-Supervised Descriptor (SSCD)1. On the Facebook AI Image Similarity Challenge 2021 benchmark (DISC21), comprising one million reference images and 50,000 manipulated queries designed to evaluate copy detection across complex distortions, SSCD outperformed baseline copy detection and self-supervised architectures1. Standard SimCLR achieves a micro-average precision (![][image9]) of ![][image10], while DINO achieves ![][image11]1. In contrast, an SSCD ResNet-50 model trained on DISC data using advanced augmentations and mixup achieves a ![][image9] of ![][image12] and a score-normalized ![][image13] of ![][image14]1. The larger SSCD ResNeXt-101 (![][image15]) configuration reaches a score-normalized ![][image13] of ![][image16]1.

The structural performance of SSCD is driven by three specific architectural mechanisms:

![][image17]

The training objective augments the standard contrastive InfoNCE loss with a differential entropy regularization term ![][image18], scaled by hyperparameter ![][image19]1. In unregularized contrastive learning, representations suffer from dimensional collapse, where the learned embeddings concentrate along a lower-dimensional sub-manifold of the hypersphere1. Differential entropy regularization penalizes non-uniformity across the embedding distribution, driving the representations toward a uniform distribution across the entire surface of the unit hypersphere1. This uniform coverage ensures that distance metrics behave consistently across disparate regions of the latent space, enabling a single global similarity threshold to function reliably across the entire database without regional calibration distortions1.

SSCD replaces standard spatial average pooling with Generalized Mean (GeM) pooling prior to the final ![][image20] normalization layer1. GeM pooling computes:

![][image21]

where ![][image22] represents the spatial feature map grid and ![][image23] is a learnable pooling parameter1. As ![][image23] increases beyond 1, the operation transitions toward max-pooling, emphasizing localized activations produced by distinct visual elements (such as pavement cracks, curb fractures, or utility cover markings) while attenuating diffuse background activations (such as uniform gravel beds or cloudless sky)1.

SSCD incorporates a cutmix- and mixup-aware InfoNCE formulation that accommodates synthetic image compositions during self-supervised pretraining1. Standard contrastive frameworks treat any blended image as a separate negative instance, which undermines representation learning when applied to composite images1. SSCD explicitly accounts for visual overlap, allowing the network to recognize original sub-regions even when embedded inside digital collages, altered by borders, or partially obscured by metadata banners1.

### **Optimal Embedding Dimension**

Empirical evaluations on DISC21 confirm that 512 dimensions provides the best balance between retrieval accuracy and systems performance1. Reducing embedding dimensions down to 128 or 256 dimensions causes measurable drops in precision: an unnormalized SimCLR baseline degrades from ![][image10] to ![][image24] ![][image9] when dropping to 128 dimensions, and relational distillation studies report drops of over 5% when compressing copy-detection vectors below 256 dimensions1. Conversely, expanding embedding dimensions from 512 to 1024 dimensions yields diminishing returns (![][image13] rises from ![][image14] to ![][image16]) while doubling system memory requirements and vector search operations across large indexes1. In an enterprise municipal audit platform indexing hundreds of thousands to millions of historical images, a 512-dimensional vector stored in 32-bit single-precision floating-point format (FP32) requires 2,048 bytes per record, fitting efficiently into memory-bus caches during approximate nearest-neighbor traversals20.

### **Image Preprocessing and Scale Normalization**

The preprocessing pipeline standardizes visual inputs while preserving high-frequency forensic details:

Incoming images are loaded in standard RGB format, and any embedded EXIF orientation metadata flags are parsed to correct orientation before modifying pixel matrices.

Spatial resizing is performed using bicubic interpolation along the maximum bounding dimension to a resolution of 512 pixels, preserving the native aspect ratio without non-linear stretching. Symmetric zero-padding is applied to the shorter dimension to yield a uniform ![][image25] square input tensor. Reflection or border-clamp padding is avoided to prevent synthetic edge gradients from polluting convolutional boundary layers.

Pixel color channels are normalized to zero mean and unit variance using standard ImageNet parameters:

![][image26]

### **Augmentation Robustness**

In municipal fraud scenarios, submitted photographs undergo varying transformations designed to evade audit discovery3:

Contractors frequently crop photographs to eliminate identifiable surrounding landmarks, such as utility poles, street numbers, or parked fleet vehicles3. SSCD’s combination of GeM pooling and aggressive crop-augmentation pretraining preserves feature activations from local regions, maintaining reliable retrieval even when only 20% of the original content remains1.

Standard convolutional neural networks are not inherently equivariant to arbitrary spatial rotations12. To mitigate evasion via image reorientation, the retrieval pipeline applies Test-Time Augmentation (TTA)18. During inference, embeddings are computed across four orthogonal rotations (![][image27]) and horizontal reflections, or extracted descriptors are averaged post\-![][image20] normalization, ensuring robust retrieval across rotated submissions18.

Field photographs transmitted across cellular links or messaging platforms are often degraded by downsampling and aggressive lossy compression. SSCD pretraining incorporates heavy Gaussian blurring (![][image28]) alongside simulated JPEG quality degradation (![][image29]), ensuring that the resulting representations remain invariant to high-frequency DCT quantization1.

Fraudulent uploads often include digital date-and-time watermarks, camera application stamps, or artificial borders11. SSCD's entropy-regularized loss explicitly trains the model to disregard high-contrast alphanumeric overlays, maintaining focus on the underlying physical scene11.

Given two unit-normalized embedding vectors ![][image30] such that ![][image31], the cosine similarity reduces directly to the inner product:

Raw inner-product similarity scores are vulnerable to query-specific calibration drift1. In unnormalized vector search, images located in dense clusters of the latent space exhibit high raw similarity scores across a broad range of unrelated targets, creating query-dependent false alarms1. To resolve this, the architecture applies Background Score Normalization1. A static background corpus ![][image33] of ![][image34] unrelated, verified-independent municipal infrastructure images is maintained. For any query descriptor ![][image35] and reference descriptor ![][image36], the normalized similarity score is defined as:

![][image37]

where ![][image38] and ![][image39] represent the mean and standard deviation of similarity scores computed between query vector ![][image35] and all vectors in the background corpus:

![][image40]

This standardization scales candidate scores into query-independent standard scores, making a single decision threshold reliable across the full operational archive1.

### **Threshold Selection and Empirical Calibration**

Operating decision thresholds are established using Neyman-Pearson statistical criteria calibrated on the DISC21 validation suite and historical municipal image corpora1. System responses are separated into three functional audit classifications:

A score-normalized threshold of ![][image41] operates as the candidate selection gate1. This boundary prioritizes recall (![][image42]), funneling all potential copies into downstream geometric verification while filtering out irrelevant records.

A score-normalized threshold of ![][image43] triggers an automated fraud review alert1. Calibrated to achieve a false-positive rate below ![][image44], this threshold identifies pairs with high likelihood of shared provenance, initiating administrative payment holds pending spatial inspection.

A score-normalized threshold of ![][image45] identifies near-exact digital duplicates1. Candidates exceeding this boundary exhibit bit-level identity or trivial format transcoding, allowing the system to reject the submission without requiring full geometric verification.

## **Scalable Indexing, Storage Footprints, and Cross-Contract Retrieval**

### **Approximate Nearest-Neighbor (ANN) Index Scaling**

To evaluate infrastructure performance as municipal archives expand from localized pilot programs to statewide oversight databases, indexing mechanisms must be evaluated across dimensional memory profiles, query latencies, and search recall targets14.

&nbsp;

| Repository Scale | Index Architecture | Memory Footprint (Vectors \+ Index Overhead) | Search Latency (p95​) | Recall@1 Target | Re-indexing Overhead & Ingestion Characteristics |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **10,000 images** | IndexFlatIP (Exhaustive Inner Product) | ![][image46] raw vectors20 | ![][image47] | ![][image48] (Exact) | Zero training phase; zero quantization error; immediate sequential vector append20. |
| **100,000 images** | IndexFlatIP or IndexHNSW32 | Flat: ![][image49] HNSW32: ![][image49] \[cite: 20\] | Flat: ![][image50] HNSW32: ![][image47] | Flat: ![][image48] HNSW: ![][image51] | Fully in-memory; HNSW graph requires no global index rebuilds; near-zero query latency14. |
| **1,000,000 images** | IndexHNSW32 | ![][image52] \[cite: 20\] | ![][image53] | ![][image51] | Modest memory footprint; resides easily in standard server RAM; avoids vector quantization loss14. |
| **10,000,000 images** | IndexIVF4096,PQ64 with HNSW Coarse Quantizer | ![][image49] (PQ codes) ![][image54] \[cite: 20\] | ![][image55] | ![][image51] (Pre-rerank) | Product Quantization compresses vectors to 64 bytes; requires k-means training across 1M samples; periodic rebalancing needed14. |

For repositories up to one million photographs, an unquantized IndexHNSW32 on 512-dimensional FP32 vectors provides the best operational balance14. Maintaining one million 512-dimensional vectors in single-precision floating-point requires 1.95 GB of raw storage, while HNSW graph links introduce an additional 244 MB of index overhead, totaling approximately 2.20 GB20. Because this structure fits comfortably within host RAM, the system eliminates the recall degradation and hyperparameter tuning associated with vector quantization methods like Product Quantization (PQ)14.

### **Incremental Indexing and Append Dynamics**

Municipal evidence systems handle continuous write workloads. Field inspectors and contractors submit verification photographs throughout the workday, requiring immediate index updates so that new images can both query historical records and serve as reference points for subsequent submissions.

Inverted File (IVF) index architectures require an offline training step to calculate Voronoi cluster centroids via k-means clustering across a representative vector sample14. Dynamically appending new vectors to an IVF index without updating centroids causes centroid drift and cluster skew, which degrades retrieval recall over time unless the full index is rebuilt.

In contrast, IndexHNSW32 natively supports continuous incremental insertions without requiring batch retraining. Incoming descriptors are integrated directly into the hierarchical proximity graph via greedy search and bidirectional link updates, maintaining sub-5 millisecond retrieval latencies without requiring service restarts or index rebuilds.

### **Cross-Contract Search Topology**

Fraudulent contractors frequently exploit organizational silos by submitting identical photographs across different municipal agencies, separate administrative contracts, or distinct funding cycles3. The search topology must support both scoped contract validation and global deduplication:

A unified, multi-tenant vector space is maintained across all historical and current contracts. Embeddings are stored in an enterprise vector engine (such as Milvus, Qdrant, or partitioned Faiss instances) alongside structured metadata payloads:

| Payload Attribute | Schema Type | Operational Audit Utility |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| image\_id | UUIDv4 (String) | Unique visual evidence identifier |
| contract\_id | String (Indexed) | Municipal contract identifier for scoped retrieval |
| vendor\_id | String (Indexed) | Contractor tax/business identifier for cross-vendor fraud tracking |
| work\_type | Low-cardinality Enum | Specific category (e.g., ASPHALT\_REPAIR, SIDEWALK\_POUR) |
| capture\_timestamp | ISO-8601 UTC | Temporal validation against invoice dates |
| geo\_coordinates | GeoJSON WGS84 Point | Spatial proximity bounds for site verification |

Auditing procedures operate across two verification modes:

Scoped Intra-Contract Validation limits the search using a boolean metadata filter (contract\_id \== CURRENT\_CONTRACT), verifying that the submission does not duplicate earlier milestones within the same project.

Global Cross-Contract Deduplication bypasses metadata filters to query the entire historical vector index. This sweeps historical archives to identify visual copies submitted under earlier fiscal cycles, across different municipal departments, or by separate corporate entities, detecting broader patterns of duplicate billing.

## **Candidate Verification and False-Positive Suppression**

While global SSCD vector search efficiently narrows down candidate pairs from millions of records to the top ![][image56] nearest neighbors, global descriptors remain vulnerable to hard negatives1. These hard negatives occur when two distinct physical sites share similar visual compositions—such as newly cast concrete curbs, standard-issue storm drain grates, or identical municipal utility vehicles3. To prevent false accusations, the system deploys a two-stage verification cascade: global vector retrieval followed by fine-grained geometric registration3.

### **Local Feature Matching and Geometric Inlier Filtering**

Candidate pairs returned by the global ANN search are routed to a spatial verification engine that evaluates fine-grained geometric consistency:

Local keypoints and feature descriptors are extracted using SuperPoint21. SuperPoint leverages a fully convolutional network trained to identify repeatable interest points and generate 256-dimensional local descriptors conditioned on spatial structural context, remaining robust across lighting changes, surface wear, and camera perspective shifts12.

Keypoint correspondence between candidate image pairs is resolved using LightGlue21. LightGlue applies cross-attention and self-attention mechanisms to refine feature representations while adaptively pruning matchable keypoints across network layers21. LightGlue achieves an AUC@5° of ![][image57] (outperforming SuperGlue’s ![][image58]) with an adaptive inference latency of 22 milliseconds per image pair, making it well-suited for interactive candidate verification21.

Candidate keypoint correspondences are processed through a robust estimator (such as MAGSAC++ or USAC) to fit a planar homography matrix ![][image59]:

![][image60]

A candidate pair is certified as an authentic instance copy if and only if it satisfies three structural criteria:

* The absolute number of geometrically verified inliers meets ![][image61].  
* The inlier ratio relative to putative matches satisfies ![][image62].  
* The fitted homography corresponds to a non-degenerate transformation, filtering out rank-deficient or severely warped coordinate mappings.

### **Resolution of System Error Modes**

Hard negatives typically share macroscopic layouts or foreground objects while background details differ3. Standard municipal equipment or prefabricated utility fixtures will match across isolated keypoints, but the surrounding scene context (such as unique asphalt aggregate, pavement crack networks, or surrounding curbs) fails to satisfy a consistent planar homography3. This geometric inconsistency suppresses false positives, filtering out non-identical scenes that share visual characteristics3.

False negatives predominantly occur under extreme cropping or perspective alterations3. When a submitted photograph captures less than 20% of an original image, the global SSCD descriptor vector can drift, causing its normalized similarity score to fall into the ambiguous range (![][image63])3. To address this, the pipeline applies Multi-Crop Query Expansion to borderline queries18. The query image is partitioned into overlapping quadrants and a centered crop, generating a 5-view sub-image set18. Each sub-crop is queried independently against the index, recovering candidate matches that may be obscured within the full global frame18.

## **Forensic Tampering, Metadata Consistency, and Provenance Analysis**

Beyond detecting unmodified or cropped duplicate photographs, the architecture verifies whether submitted evidence has been manipulated, spliced, or synthetically altered3.

### **Forensic Splicing and Tampering Localization**

Digital image manipulation often involves compositing elements from separate sources, such as splicing a photo of completed asphalt patching into an image of an uncompleted job site, or using inpainting to remove visible infrastructure damage6. Forensic detection combines high-level RGB features with low-level sensor noise patterns25.

The primary network for this stage is TruFor (CVPR 2023\)25. TruFor combines high-level RGB features with a learned noise-sensitive fingerprint (Noiseprint++) using a cross-modal transformer fusion architecture25. The Noiseprint++ stream models camera sensor artifacts, photo-response non-uniformity (PRNU), and camera processing pipeline characteristics26. When an image is manipulated via copy-move, splicing, or inpainting, the altered region exhibits statistical discontinuities relative to the camera's baseline sensor noise pattern24.

TruFor produces three distinct operational outputs:

* A pixel-level manipulation probability heatmap ![][image64] identifying altered regions26.  
* An overall image integrity score ![][image65] reflecting capture authenticity26.  
* A spatial reliability map ![][image66] flagging areas where forensic analysis is less confident due to saturated highlights, deep shadows, or low-texture regions26.

On standard forensic benchmarks, TruFor demonstrates consistent localization performance, achieving an Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC) of 0.888 on CASIA, 0.760 on Coverage, and 0.960 on NIST1624.

This analysis is complemented by Compression Artifact Tracing Networks (such as CAT-Net), which evaluate double JPEG compression artifacts in Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) coefficients and 8x8 block boundary grids25. Splicing operations routinely introduce inconsistent compression characteristics when content saved at quality ![][image67] is composited into an image saved at quality ![][image68], leaving detectable boundary artifacts25.

Deploying forensic detectors in municipal settings requires adjusting decision thresholds to account for class imbalance25. In real-world document and infrastructure tampering, manipulated regions often occupy under 3% of the total pixel area25. Applying standard decision thresholds (![][image69]) can lead to high false-negative rates25. Operating boundaries are calibrated using extreme-value statistical profiling, alerting when an anomalous region covers a contiguous block of at least ![][image70] pixels with a local manipulation probability exceeding ![][image71].

### **Metadata and EXIF Cross-Consistency Analysis**

Automated metadata checks provide computationally efficient integrity signals prior to neural network processing:

The EXIF directory is inspected for processing history tags, such as Software, ProcessingSoftware, and History. The presence of desktop editing suites (such as Adobe Photoshop, GIMP, or Canva) or mobile retouching applications flags the image for manual forensic review.

The system evaluates temporal consistency across internal timestamp fields, verifying alignment between DateTimeOriginal, DateTimeDigitized, and container-level file modification timestamps. Mismatches between GPS-derived atomic timestamps (UTC) and local device clock entries often indicate fabricated timelines.

Reported camera parameters—including Make, Model, ExifImageWidth, FocalLength, and LensSpecification—are validated against known sensor hardware profiles. Inconsistencies indicate that metadata headers may have been transferred from a different device.

Standard digital camera pipelines embed a low-resolution JPEG preview thumbnail directly into the EXIF container structure. Consumer editing applications frequently alter full-resolution pixel arrays while leaving the embedded thumbnail unchanged. The pipeline decompresses the embedded thumbnail and computes its perceptual hash; a high Hamming distance between the thumbnail and the primary image indicates that the image was modified after capture.

### **Cryptographic Provenance via C2PA**

The technical foundation for verifying original image capture is the Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) standard30. Modern mobile devices and enterprise camera applications can generate signed JUMBF (JPEG Universal Metadata Box Format) manifests at the moment of image capture31.

The ingestion pipeline integrates the C2PA Python SDK (c2pa-python) to validate cryptographic provenance manifests30:

&nbsp;

&nbsp;

&nbsp;

Python

import c2pa

def verify\_c2pa\_provenance(image\_path: str) \-\> dict:  
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;try:  
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;reader \= c2pa.Reader.from\_file(image\_path)  
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;manifest\_data \= reader.json()  
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;active\_manifest \= reader.active\_manifest()  
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;is\_signature\_valid \= reader.validate\_signatures()  
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;  
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;return {  
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;"c2pa\_manifest\_found": True,  
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;"signature\_valid": is\_signature\_valid,  
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;"claim\_generator": active\_manifest.get("claim\_generator\_info"),  
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;"signing\_authority": active\_manifest.get("signature\_info", {}).get("issuer"),  
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;"provenance\_assertions": active\_manifest.get("assertions", \[\])  
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;}  
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;except c2pa.C2paError:  
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;return {  
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;"c2pa\_manifest\_found": False,  
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;"signature\_valid": False,  
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;"claim\_generator": None,  
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;"signing\_authority": None,  
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;"provenance\_assertions": \[\]  
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;}

A valid C2PA manifest cryptographically binds hardware-attested capture coordinates, camera serial numbers, and SHA-256 pixel hashes (c2pa.hash.data) signed by accredited Certificate Authorities31. When an incoming image includes a valid C2PA manifest with an unbroken certificate chain and no unauthorized downstream editing assertions, it can bypass expensive heuristic tampering checks, reducing overall verification compute costs31.

## **Visual Change Detection: Before-and-After Evidence Verification**

Municipal contracts frequently require contractors to provide paired "Before" and "After" photographs to verify milestone completion (such as an open roadway trench versus a completed asphalt pour)4. Common fraudulent patterns in this context include submitting identical photographs twice, submitting two photographs captured in rapid succession from slightly different angles without performing actual work, or submitting photographs from different physical locations7.

To verify genuine physical progress, the architecture implements a multi-stage change-detection pipeline evaluating both spatial alignment and surface state transitions:

Image registration begins by aligning the Before Image (![][image72]) and After Image (![][image73]) into a shared coordinate frame21. SuperPoint keypoints are matched using LightGlue, and MAGSAC++ fits a planar homography ![][image74] that registers ![][image72] directly to ![][image73]21. If the number of spatial inliers is insufficient (![][image75]), the system issues a **Location Mismatch Alert**, indicating that the contractor submitted photographs of two entirely different physical locations.

Following geometric alignment, the registered images are evaluated using the Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM) across the overlapping field of view:

![][image76]

If the structural similarity exceeds ![][image77], the scene exhibits near-identical structural characteristics. This triggers a **Duplicate Submission Alert**, indicating that the contractor submitted duplicate photographs with minor lighting or compression differences rather than performing actual work.

To distinguish genuine work progress from environmental shifts (such as changing weather, moving cast shadows, or passing traffic), the system isolates the target work zone ![][image78] using a semantic segmentation model. Within this defined region, local token features are extracted using a DINOv2-ViT backbone9. The local physical change score is computed as the mean cosine distance between registered feature tokens:

![][image79]

A submission is certified as **Verified Physical Progress** when it satisfies geometric alignment (![][image61]), exhibits background stability (![][image80]), and demonstrates measurable structural transformation within the target work zone (![][image81]).

| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Site Registration** | Homography Inliers (![][image82])21 | ![][image83] | **Location Mismatch**: The photographs represent different physical locations. |
| **Duplicate Check** | Registered SSIM | ![][image84] | **Duplicate Submission Fraud**: Identical photograph submitted twice. |
| **Short-Interval Check** | Keypoint Stability \+ Temporal EXIF | ![][image1] inliers, ![][image85] | **Suspicious Inaction**: Consecutive captures without physical intervention. |
| **Progress Validation** | Work Zone Feature Delta (![][image86])9 | ![][image84] (with ![][image87]) | **Verified Progress**: Legitimate structural work completed. |

## **End-to-End System Pipeline Design**

The complete verification architecture coordinates evidence processing from raw multi-part upload through to finding generation:

The ingestion endpoint accepts multi-part HTTP requests containing image binaries alongside operational metadata (including Contract ID, Vendor ID, Geographic Coordinates, Submission Timestamp, and Claim Type).

The file byte stream is parsed to extract EXIF, XMP, and JUMBF metadata blocks. Any embedded C2PA manifests are evaluated for signature validity and certificate chain integrity30. If the image lacks cryptographic provenance, the pipeline parses standard EXIF tags, checking camera hardware consistency and comparing the embedded preview thumbnail against the main image raster. Spatial dimensions are normalized via bicubic interpolation along the maximum axis to 512 pixels with zero-padding to yield a ![][image25] RGB tensor.

The normalized image tensor is passed to an SSCD TorchScript inference model (ResNet-50 backbone with GeM pooling, ![][image88])1. The model extracts a 512-dimensional continuous feature vector, which is immediately ![][image20]\-normalized1.

The 512-dimensional vector queries an in-memory Faiss IndexHNSW32 structure using inner-product distance14. The query executes across two distinct scopes: a contract-isolated search for duplicate submissions within the current project, and a global cross-contract search covering all historical municipal evidence. The retrieval stage returns the top ![][image56] nearest neighbors exceeding the candidate threshold of ![][image41]1.

Candidates exceeding the candidate threshold are evaluated using SuperPoint keypoint extraction and LightGlue attention matching21. The system fits a planar homography using MAGSAC++; candidate pairs with at least 25 inliers and an inlier ratio of at least ![][image89] are flagged as confirmed image duplicates12.

If the submission is not a duplicate, it is processed through the TruFor cross-modal network25. TruFor computes an overall image integrity score ![][image90] and outputs a pixel-level manipulation probability map26. Connected regions larger than ![][image70] pixels with manipulation probabilities above ![][image91] are flagged for splicing or inpainting.

For paired milestone submissions (Before/After claims), the registered change-detection module evaluates site co-registration and computes the feature change score ![][image86] across the segmented work zone9.

All verification findings, similarity metrics, geometric homographies, and forensic heatmaps are compiled into a structured JSON record and assembled into a PDF evidence package for municipal review.

&nbsp;

| Pipeline Stage | Processing Module | Computational Substrate | Nominal Latency (p95​) | Primary Operational Output |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **1\. Ingestion & Preprocessing** | Container parsing, EXIF check, C2PA validation, aspect-preserving resize30 | CPU (Multi-threaded) | ![][image92] | Normalized ![][image93] tensor; metadata integrity report31 |
| **2\. Global Feature Extraction** | SSCD ResNet-50 TorchScript (sscd\_disc\_mixup)1 | GPU (CUDA / TensorRT) | ![][image50] | ![][image94]\-dimensional ![][image20]\-normalized vector1 |
| **3\. ANN Vector Retrieval** | Faiss IndexHNSW32 (![][image95], ![][image96])14 | RAM / Host Memory | ![][image50] | Top ![][image97] candidate image IDs with normalized scores1 |
| **4\. Geometric Verification** | SuperPoint keypoint extraction \+ LightGlue feature matcher \+ MAGSAC++21 | GPU (CUDA) | ![][image92] per candidate pair21 | Inlier count, inlier ratio, and fitted ![][image98] homography matrix12 |
| **5\. Forensic Integrity Analysis** | TruFor cross-modal fusion (RGB \+ Noiseprint++)25 | GPU (CUDA) | ![][image92] | Image integrity score ![][image90], pixel manipulation mask26 |
| **6\. Before/After Change Detection** | Keypoint alignment \+ Semantic work mask \+ DINOv2 patch token delta9 | GPU (CUDA) | ![][image92] | Progress classification (Location Mismatch, Duplicate, Legitimate Progress) |
| **7\. Finding Generation** | Audit record synthesis and PDF dossier compilation | CPU (Worker Node) | ![][image92] | JSON finding schema and forensic PDF evidence package |

## **Implementation Phasing: Hackathon MVP Versus Enterprise Production**

To deliver a working system within a compressed hackathon timeline while establishing a clear upgrade path toward enterprise deployment, system components are partitioned across two development phases:

&nbsp;

| Architectural Subsystem | Hackathon MVP Deployment Scope | Enterprise Production Scope | Technical Rationale |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Instance Copy Detection** | Pretrained SSCD ResNet-50 TorchScript (sscd\_disc\_mixup.torchscript.pt)19 | Fine-tuned SSCD ResNeXt-101 with municipal hard-negative calibration1 | Pretrained SSCD TorchScript provides instant inference without training; handles crops, blur, and color shifts out-of-the-box1. |
| **Vector Indexing & Search** | In-memory Faiss IndexFlatIP (Single-node Python service)20 | Distributed Qdrant or Milvus cluster with metadata-filtered IndexHNSW32 \[cite: 14, 20\] | Flat inner-product index provides 100% exact recall and ![][image47] search across ![][image99] demo records without cluster management20. |
| **Spatial Verification** | SIFT \+ OpenCV RANSAC (or lightweight LightGlue ONNX)21 | SuperPoint \+ LightGlue attention engine accelerated via TensorRT22 | OpenCV SIFT/RANSAC requires zero specialized weights and minimal dependencies, providing robust geometric proof for presentation demos. |
| **Tampering & Splicing** | EXIF container parsing \+ Error Level Analysis (ELA) via Pillow35 | Full TruFor RGB \+ Noiseprint++ cross-modal segmentation pipeline25 | ELA and EXIF parsing execute in ![][image100] on CPU, reliably highlighting JPEG quality mismatches without requiring GPU overhead35. |
| **Provenance Tracking** | Standard EXIF validation & embedded thumbnail hash matching | Cryptographic C2PA validation via c2pa-python against trust anchors30 | C2PA requires integration with signed hardware camera workflows; EXIF/thumbnail mismatches demonstrate the concept without enterprise PKI30. |
| **Before / After Analysis** | Homography alignment via keypoints \+ global SSIM difference threshold | Semantic segmentation masking (work zone isolation) \+ DINOv2 patch delta9 | Keypoint alignment \+ SSIM clearly differentiates identical re-uploads from physical scene modifications with minimal code complexity. |
| **Audit Dossier Output** | Interactive Streamlit/FastAPI dashboard displaying matching pairs & JSON findings | Asynchronous task queue (Celery/Redis) generating signed PDF audit packages | Focuses hackathon delivery on real-time visual inspection, immediate query feedback, and fraud demonstration. |

For the hackathon MVP, the system focuses on three core capabilities: SSCD-based vector retrieval to identify duplicate submissions, OpenCV geometric verification to visualize matched keypoint alignments, and EXIF/ELA analysis to detect manipulated metadata and compression inconsistencies. This configuration runs efficiently on standard hardware without complex infrastructure dependencies.

For enterprise production, the architecture expands to include distributed vector storage (Milvus or Qdrant) with HNSW indexing, full TruFor cross-modal splicing detection, C2PA cryptographic provenance verification, and semantic-guided change detection for Before/After validation.

## **Architectural Conclusions and Strategic Recommendations**

Deploying a computer vision evidence verification pipeline for municipal oversight requires a clear separation between semantic classification models and instance-level copy detection frameworks. General vision-language models such as CLIP and self-supervised models such as DINOv2 are optimized for semantic grouping; when applied to municipal verification, they struggle to differentiate between distinct instances of standard infrastructure assets like asphalt patches, guardrails, or concrete curbs6.

The primary recommendation for MuniAudit-AI is to establish Meta AI's SSCD as the global feature extraction backbone1. Its combination of differential entropy regularization and GeM pooling preserves local structural activations while maintaining a uniform representation distribution across the latent space1. This architecture provides robustness against common evasion techniques—including spatial cropping, rotations, and severe lossy compression—outperforming conventional perceptual hashing and standard self-supervised baselines1.

To eliminate false-positive fraud allegations caused by visually repetitive infrastructure, the architecture implements a two-stage verification cascade. Fast approximate nearest-neighbor retrieval over 512-dimensional SSCD embeddings acts as an initial candidate filter, followed by fine-grained spatial verification using SuperPoint and LightGlue1. This geometric verification stage enforces rigid planar homography constraints, filtering out visually similar hard negatives and ensuring that formal audit flags reflect genuine photographic duplicates12.

For evidence lifecycle management, municipal archives up to one million photographs are best served by an in-memory IndexHNSW32 structure14. This approach avoids vector quantization loss, maintains sub-5 millisecond query latencies, and supports real-time incremental vector insertions as new work orders are submitted14. Operating search queries across both contract-scoped and global historical indices ensures that contractors cannot evade detection by reusing visual evidence across different municipal departments or accounting periods3.

Finally, the verification framework incorporates pixel-level tampering localization via TruFor and cryptographic provenance validation via C2PA26. By combining global copy detection, geometric verification, forensic tampering analysis, and metadata provenance, the proposed pipeline provides an automated defense against fraudulent billing, protecting public funds and maintaining evidentiary integrity across municipal infrastructure programs.
